## Before we start {.unnumbered}

Make sure your folder structure looks like this before running anything:

```         
intro_to_gis/
├── exercises_code/
│   └── ex_1.qmd       <- this file goes here
└── data/
    └── raw/
        ├── tram_lines.csv
        └── markets.csv
```

Download the data files from OPAL and place them in `data/raw/` before the session.

### Packages for this session {.unnumbered}

```{r setup}
library(pacman)

pacman::p_load(
  ggplot2,
  dplyr,
  sf,
  raster,
  rnaturalearth,
  rnaturalearthdata,
  here,
  terra,
  tidyr
)

here::i_am("exercises_code/ex_1.qmd")
```

## Vector data and the `sf` package

### What is vector data?

Geographic vector data represent features in space using **points**, **lines**, and **polygons** — all defined within a Coordinate Reference System (CRS).

| Geometry type       | Built from                   | Example                     |
|---------------------|------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Point               | A single coordinate pair     | A market location           |
| Linestring          | Two or more connected points | A tram line                 |
| Polygon             | A closed sequence of points  | A district boundary         |
| Geometry collection | Mix of the above             | A city with roads and parks |

Every spatial object carries a `geometry` column containing coordinate pairs (longitude, latitude).

### The `sf` package

The **simple features** (`sf`) package is the standard for working with vector data in R. It supports 17 geometry types and integrates naturally with `dplyr` and `ggplot2`.

Key geometry constructor functions:

-   `st_point()` — creates a point from a numeric vector
-   `st_linestring()` — creates a line from a matrix of coordinates
-   `st_polygon()` — creates a polygon from a list of coordinate matrices
-   `st_multipoint()`, `st_multilinestring()` — multi-part variants
-   `st_sfc()` — combines geometries into a simple feature column
-   `st_sf()` — combines an `sfc` with a data frame to make a full spatial dataset

### Creating geometries from scratch

```{r geometries}
# --- Points (from numeric vectors) ---
p_1 <- st_point(c(5, 2))          # 2D point (X, Y)
p_2 <- st_point(c(7, 3, 5))       # 3D point (X, Y, Z)
p_3 <- st_point(c(8, 1, 4), dim = "XYM")    # X, Y + measure
p_4 <- st_point(c(6, 3, 5, 9), dim = "XYZM") # X, Y, Z + measure

# --- Multipoints (from a matrix) ---
multi_point_matrix <- rbind(c(4, 5), c(6, 4), c(9, 5))
multipoint <- st_multipoint(multi_point_matrix)
plot(multipoint, main = "Multipoint")

# --- Linestring (from a matrix) ---
line_matrix <- rbind(c(4, 5), c(6, 4), c(9, 5))
linestring <- st_linestring(line_matrix)
plot(linestring, main = "Linestring")

# --- Polygon with a hole (from a list of matrices) ---
border <- rbind(c(1, 5), c(2, 2), c(4, 1), c(4, 4), c(1, 5))
hole   <- rbind(c(2, 4), c(3, 4), c(3, 3), c(2, 3), c(2, 4))
polygon <- st_polygon(list(border, hole))
plot(polygon, main = "Polygon with hole")

# --- Geometry collection ---
geom_collection <- st_geometrycollection(list(multipoint, linestring))
plot(geom_collection, main = "Geometry collection")
```

### Simple feature columns (`sfc`)

An `sfc` object is a list of geometries sharing the same CRS — it is the `geometry` column of any spatial data frame.

```{r sfc}
# Combine two points into a single sfc
points_sfc <- st_sfc(p_1, p_2)
print(points_sfc)

# Always useful: check the geometry type of any spatial object
st_geometry_type(linestring)
st_geometry_type(polygon)
```

::: callout-note
## Quick check

What does `st_geometry_type(geom_collection)` return? Run it and think about why.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)

A CRS defines how coordinates map onto the Earth's surface. Two broad families:

-   **Geographic CRS** (e.g. WGS84 / EPSG:4326): coordinates in degrees of latitude and longitude. Standard in economics and most global datasets.
-   **Projected CRS** (e.g. ESRI:54009 Mollweide): coordinates in metres on a flat surface. Better for distance calculations and area measurements.

### Checking and setting a CRS

```{r projections}
# Default CRS is NA — no projection assigned yet
st_crs(multipoint)

# Wrap in sfc first, then assign WGS84
multipoint_sfc <- st_sfc(multipoint)
multipoint_wgs <- st_set_crs(multipoint_sfc, 4326)
st_crs(multipoint_wgs)
```

::: callout-warning
## st_set_crs() vs st_transform()

`st_set_crs()` **assigns** a CRS without touching the coordinates — use it only when the data has no CRS at all.\
`st_transform()` **reprojects** the coordinates from one CRS to another — use this when you need to change projection.\
Confusing the two is a very common source of silent errors.
:::

### Reprojecting a world map

```{r reprojections}
world_map <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")

# Default CRS
st_crs(world_map)$epsg

# Plot in default WGS84
plot(world_map["sovereignt"], main = "WGS84 (EPSG:4326)")

# Reproject to Mollweide equal-area projection
world_mollweide <- st_transform(world_map, crs = "ESRI:54009")
plot(world_mollweide["sovereignt"], main = "Mollweide (ESRI:54009)")
```

::: callout-tip
## Why does projection matter in economics?

If you are computing distances, areas, or spatial weights matrices, the results will differ depending on the CRS. WGS84 works well for global visualisations; for area calculations within a country, a local projected CRS (e.g. ETRS89 for Germany) is more appropriate.
:::

## Working with real data — Dresden

We use data from the [Dresden Open Data Portal](https://opendata.dresden.de/informationsportal/). The datasets contain a column called `geom` storing geometries in **WKT (Well-Known Text)** format, which `sf` can read directly.

### Tram lines

```{r tram-data}
# Load the CSV — note the semicolon separator
tram_lines <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "tram_lines.csv"), sep = ";")

# Inspect before converting
head(tram_lines)

# Convert to sf using the WKT geometry column
tram_lines_sf <- st_as_sf(tram_lines, wkt = "geom")

# Check what we got
names(tram_lines_sf)
st_crs(tram_lines_sf)
st_geometry_type(tram_lines_sf) |> table()
```

```{r tram-plot}
# Quick base plot
plot(tram_lines_sf["strasse"], main = "Dresden tram lines")

# Better: ggplot with geom_sf
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = tram_lines_sf, aes(color = historie)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(AKT = "steelblue", NEU = "salmon")) +
  labs(title = "Dresden tram network", color = "Status") +
  theme_void()
```

### Markets

```{r market-data}
market    <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "markets.csv"), sep = ";")
market_sf <- st_as_sf(market, wkt = "geom")

# What geometry type are markets?
st_geometry_type(market_sf) |> table()

plot(market_sf["id"], main = "Dresden markets")
```

### Combining layers

Because both datasets share the same CRS, we can overlay them in a single `ggplot` call — no merging needed.

```{r combined-plot}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = tram_lines_sf, color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = market_sf, color = "firebrick", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Dresden: tram lines and markets") +
  theme_void()
```

::: callout-caution
## Exercise 1 — Your turn

The combined map above has no basemap, so it is hard to orient yourself.

1.  Check whether the two datasets share the same CRS. If not, reproject one of them.
2.  Add a `subtitle` to the plot that shows the CRS (hint: use `st_crs()` to extract it and paste it into the subtitle string).
3.  **Bonus:** Add a north arrow or scale bar using the `ggspatial` package (`annotation_scale()` and `annotation_north_arrow()`).
:::

## Raster data and the `raster` package

Raster data represent the world as a **grid of equally sized cells**, each containing one value. Think of them as images where every pixel stores a measurement (elevation, temperature, vegetation index, etc.).

Key properties of a raster:

| Property   | Meaning                      |
|------------|------------------------------|
| Extent     | The geographic bounding box  |
| Resolution | Cell size (e.g. 0.5° × 0.5°) |
| CRS        | How coordinates are defined  |
| Values     | What each cell stores        |

### Building a raster from scratch

```{r raster-basic}
raster_extent <- extent(-1.5, 1.5, -1.5, 1.5)

our_raster <- raster(
  nrows = 6, ncols = 6,
  res   = 0.5,
  ext   = raster_extent,
  vals  = 1:36
)

plot(our_raster, main = "6×6 raster, resolution 0.5")
```

### Resolution and granularity

```{r raster-resolution}
# Finer resolution = more cells = more detail
fine_raster <- raster(
  nrows = 60, ncols = 60,
  res   = 0.05,
  ext   = raster_extent
)
values(fine_raster) <- 1:ncell(fine_raster)

plot(fine_raster, main = "60×60 raster, resolution 0.05")
```

::: callout-note
## Resolution in practice

Online data sources typically report resolution in degrees. A 0.5° raster corresponds to cells of roughly 55 km × 55 km at the equator. A 0.05° raster (\~5.5 km cells) is ten times finer and ten times larger in file size.\
When downloading data, always check the resolution against your analytical needs — finer is not always better.
:::

::: callout-caution
## Exercise 2 — Raster resolution

1.  Create a raster with the same extent as `our_raster` but with resolution `0.25`. How many cells does it have? Verify with `ncell()`.
2.  Create another raster with resolution `1.0`. Plot both side by side using `par(mfrow = c(1, 2))`.
3.  What is the relationship between resolution and number of cells? Write it as a formula in a comment.
:::

### Projections in raster data

```{r raster-crs}
data(volcano)
volcano_raster <- raster(volcano)

# No CRS yet
projection(volcano_raster)

# Assign WGS84 using proj4 string
proj4_wgs84 <- "+proj=longlat +datum=WGS84 +ellps=WGS84 +towgs84=0,0,0"
projection(volcano_raster) <- proj4_wgs84

projection(volcano_raster)
raster::plot(volcano_raster, main = "Volcano raster")
```

```{r raster-ggplot}
# Higher quality plot via ggplot (requires converting to data frame first)
volcano_df <- as.data.frame(volcano_raster, xy = TRUE)

ggplot(volcano_df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = layer)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = terrain.colors(10)) +
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude",
       title = "Volcano — ggplot rendering", fill = "Elevation") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## The `terra` package

`terra` is the modern successor to both `raster` and parts of `sf`. It uses two unified data types:

-   **`SpatVector`** — equivalent to `sf` objects (vectors)
-   **`SpatRaster`** — equivalent to `raster` objects (rasters)

`terra` is generally faster than `raster` for large files and will become the standard going forward. We introduce both here because you will encounter `raster` objects in many existing papers and scripts.

### Vectors in terra

```{r terra-vector}
# Convert an sf object to SpatVector
terra_tram <- terra::vect(tram_lines_sf)

# The geometry is no longer a named column
names(terra_tram)
str(terra_tram)
```

### Rasters in terra

```{r terra-raster}
# Convert volcano to SpatRaster
terra_volcano <- terra::rast(volcano)
str(terra_volcano)
```

### Plotting in terra

Always use `terra::plot()` explicitly — the function name `plot()` is shared across many packages and calling the wrong one produces confusing errors.

```{r terra-plot}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
terra::plot(terra_tram,    col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, main = "Tram lines (SpatVector)")
terra::plot(terra_volcano, col = terrain.colors(10), main = "Volcano (SpatRaster)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

### CRS in terra

In `terra`, both `SpatVectors` and `SpatRasters` use the same functions:

-   `crs()` — inspect the CRS
-   `project()` — reproject (replaces `st_transform()` and `projectRaster()`)

```{r terra-crs}
crs(terra_tram)

# Reproject to Albers Equal Area
albers <- "+proj=aea +lat_1=29.5 +lat_2=45.5 +lat_0=37.5 +lon_0=-97.5 +datum=WGS84 +units=m"
terra_tram_albers <- project(terra_tram, albers)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
terra::plot(terra_tram,        main = "Original CRS")
terra::plot(terra_tram_albers, main = "Albers Equal Area")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: callout-caution
## Exercise 3 — Package comparison

Using the tram lines data:

1.  Check the CRS using `st_crs()` (sf), `projection()` (raster), and `crs()` (terra). Do they return the same information in the same format?
2.  Reproject the tram lines to EPSG:25833 (the standard projected CRS for Saxony/Germany) using both `st_transform()` and `terra::project()`. Plot both results — do they look the same?
3.  In your own words: what is the main practical advantage of `terra` over having separate `sf` and `raster` workflows?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Summary

|                   | sf               | raster              | terra                   |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Data type         | sf / sfc         | RasterLayer / Stack | SpatVector / SpatRaster |
| Vectors           | ✓                | ✗                   | ✓                       |
| Rasters           | ✗                | ✓                   | ✓                       |
| Check CRS         | `st_crs()`       | `projection()`      | `crs()`                 |
| Assign CRS        | `st_set_crs()`   | `projection() <-`   | `crs() <-`              |
| Reproject         | `st_transform()` | `projectRaster()`   | `project()`             |
| ggplot compatible | ✓ (geom_sf)      | needs conversion    | needs conversion        |

::: callout-tip
